The block size ZFS uses for new files, read from the library’s dataset, and the one recommended for the library from its average bitrate: 512K under 1 Mbps (music, audiobooks), 1M up to 15 Mbps (FLAC, SD to 1080p encodes), 2M up to 40 Mbps (4K encodes, 1080p remuxes) and 4M above (4K remuxes); 128K for files under 1 MB, which fit in a block or two anyway. The second best is the neighbour on the side the bitrate leans to. Ideal: the dataset uses the recommended size. Pass: it uses the second best — fine too, so a library near the line between two doesn’t flip back and forth. Warning: neither.

To fix a warning: in TrueNAS, Datasets → the library’s dataset → Edit → Advanced Options → Record Size: the recommended size. It only applies to files written afterwards; on the Optimizer page, TrueNAS compression & record size writes the existing ones again. If other libraries on the same dataset need a different size, see Media Datasets below.

What it checks: that the dataset’s record size — the largest block ZFS writes a file in — suits every library on it. Each library’s recommended size and second best come from its average bitrate (see Libraries above); one of them is Pass.

What it checks: that every file on the dataset is written in blocks of the dataset’s record size. Each health check looks at every file (their details, not their contents — a fraction of a second). Files smaller than one record don’t count: they’re a single block of their own size.

Why it matters: ZFS uses a record size only for files written after it’s set. Files written before keep their old block size — and with it the slower reads and cache use the dataset’s setting was chosen to avoid — until they’re written again.

To fix a warning: on the Optimizer page, TrueNAS compression & record size writes those files again, one at a time.

What it checks: the dataset’s compression. Video barely compresses, but fonts, the index, tags and the padding at the end of each file do — and the index is cached with the start of every file, so the smaller it is, the more fits in the cache.

Pass: ZSTD at levels 3 to 19. ZSTD-3 (plain “ZSTD” in TrueNAS) is recommended. From level 3, ZFS gives up early on what won’t compress, so video costs almost nothing to try. Higher levels make marginally smaller files but use more CPU when writing (imports, the optimizer); reading is no slower at any level. On a mostly idle NAS, a higher level is fine — your choice.

Warning: ZSTD-1 and 2 (slightly less compression, and no faster in practice), LZ4 and ZSTD-FAST (less compression), and anything else (off, GZIP — also slower to read —, ZLE, LZJB).

ZFS doesn’t write to the L2ARC directly: everything is read into RAM first, and about once a second ZFS copies a little of what’s about to leave RAM to the SSD — at most l2arc_write_max a second. Anything read from the disks faster than that leaves RAM before it’s copied, so the read was wasted. Automatic pacing reads just under that speed. Reads that come from the SSD or RAM already aren’t held back: there’s nothing to copy.

To warm up faster, raise l2arc_write_max (Health shows how); automatic pacing follows it. Warm-up’s “Run Now” runs at full speed.

These apply only when there’s an L2ARC, to all caching that needs one: warm-up, and the Prefetch choices with the grey SSD icon (the whole library’s lead-ins, the rest of a season in full…). It reads in the background at this pace and steps aside for anything below, then carries on where it left off. Prefetch’s share is one queue for every player: the newest request goes to the front, and everything in it is read in the end, even after its player stops. Caching that works on RAM alone — Now Playing Cache, and Prefetch’s smaller steps like the next episode — never waits for these, so the reads that help most are never held up.

Different disks cope with several reads at once very differently. Hard drives slow right down: the heads jump between the files, so one or two at a time finishes each sooner. SATA SSDs have no heads to move, but a single link that a few reads fill. NVMe SSDs are built for many reads at once.

Suggested: 2 for hard drives · 4 for SATA SSDs · 8 for NVMe SSDs.

The last record of a file is usually only partly filled: with a 1M record size, the end of a file might hold only 500K. ZFS keeps a record compressed only when compression saves at least 12.5%, so a record that mixes a little compressible data with a lot that isn’t (video, images) is often stored as it is.

So the optimizer puts the cover art straight after the video — it barely compresses, but it’s large enough to fill out a record — and the fonts, chapters, index and tags after it. Those compress very well, and sitting together at the very end of the file, the record that holds them is very likely to be compressed: ZSTD-3 often halves them.

The index is needed before a file can start playing, so it’s cached along with the start of every file. ZFS caches it as it’s stored on disk, compressed — so the smaller it is, the more files fit in the same cache and the longer they stay there.

How often the app asks Plex what’s playing. Each check is one small request on your own network, so the load is tiny at any of these. What changes is how quickly it reacts: when a stream starts, when someone skips (Now Playing Cache then reads from the new spot), and when a player buffers (L2ARC-only caching pauses for it).

3 seconds — a lot of music, or viewers who skip around: reacts a little sooner.
5 seconds — the best fit for most people.
10 seconds — fine for mostly movies and TV watched straight through.
30 seconds — the fewest requests, but streams and skips can be noticed up to half a minute late; short songs may be half over, and brief buffering can be missed.

Faster than 3 seconds gains little: Now Playing Cache waits for Plex’s own start-up buffer anyway.

MQTT is a common way for home automation and monitoring tools to share data, through a broker that everything connects to. Dionysus publishes everything as one JSON message on {base}/state (every {n} s, and straight away after a change), says online/offline on {base}/availability, and takes commands on {base}/set/…. Node-RED, openHAB, ioBroker, Telegraf and others can read those directly.

Security: the broker login is the lock. Use a separate login per device, use TLS if your broker offers it, and switch off “Allow control” for a watch-only connection. Broker ACLs can limit this login to the {base}/# and {prefix}/# topics.

The app uses it to tell a cache hit from a disk read (a read at least 4× faster came from cache) — that’s how warm-up reports what was already cached — to time Now Playing Cache’s automatic start, and to work out how hard background warm-up is working your disks. Plex can hold the same film on two records — one added before the other was matched, a second copy in another folder — each with its own poster, edits and watched state. Plex’s own Merge turns them into versions of one record, keeping the record’s metadata; this finds them for you. Records are the same film when they hold the very same file (a link or a copy in another folder: the same size and running time), whatever each is matched to; or when they share a match or, unmatched, when their files are named for the same title and year — and their running times agree (4% or 30 seconds, whichever is more: a different frame rate or cut of the credits; two films that merely share a title and year differ by more), and they’re the same edition (a Director’s Cut and the theatrical cut are two records on purpose), unless their files are the very same file. The record kept is the one with the most edited fields, then the most files, then the oldest. No file is touched, so a mirror isn’t affected.

It also finds the copies Plex doesn’t list at all — a second path to a listed file, or an identical copy of one (the same size and bytes at both ends): Plex’s scanner skips a file it already has under another path, so these only show on disk, taking space and getting cached and optimized twice. The copy kept is the one in a folder of its own, then the newest, then the first Plex lists — or the one you choose with the arrow between them; the others are set aside in the library’s own trash folder (on the same dataset: no copying) and Plex asked to scan. They’re deleted for good only once Plex here no longer lists them — and, with a mirror, once its Plex no longer does either (the synced folder carries the change there) — then after the hold below. Until then, each can be put back.

A hard link is one file under two paths; a symlink is a path that points at another. Plex lists only one of two paths to the same bytes, so a linked copy never shows there. Syncthing can’t carry a hard link at all: the other site gets two whole, separate copies, and once either changes the two sites no longer hold the same thing. A symlink is carried as a link, and dangles on the other side when its target isn’t in the synced folder. This tool makes each linked file a file of its own under the same path — the bytes copied beside it and swapped in, the dates kept, so Plex and the folder sync see the same file. Once every site holds plain files, Merge Duplicates and Duplicate Versions can tidy the copies safely.

The optimizer is the part of Dionysus that rewrites your media files so they suit caching: in their dataset’s record size and compression and, for MKV files, with the attachments, chapters, index and tags after the video. The Optimizer page has the choices for each library and a card for each file to optimize, with Optimize Selected.

It’s optional, and runs as a second service in this app — the only part of Dionysus that can write to your media. It does nothing on its own: it rewrites one file at a time when you press Optimize Now, checks each new file before swapping it in, and skips anything playing or just added. It has no web page and no port of its own; only this app talks to it, with a token both services share.

MP3 — MPEG-1 Layer III, from 1993, the codec that made music files small enough to share. Its psychoacoustic model is a generation behind: sharp sounds (a drum hit, a plucked string) get a smear of noise just before them (pre-echo), most encoders cut everything above 16 kHz to save bits, and the format can’t go above 320 kbps however good the source. In the listening tests Hydrogenaudio has collected, AAC and Opus are preferred to MP3 at every bitrate; at the same quality they need about a third less space.

A forced subtitle track in a language none of the audio tracks is in — or whose audio language is unknown (und), so it can’t be told. Forced subtitles show by themselves, without the viewer turning subtitles on, and are made for the audio they go with — written in its language — for three things: speech in another language than the audio’s (a foreign line in a film), words one wants to read before they’re heard (a sing-along, an anime opening), and text shown on screen (a sign, a letter, a newspaper) — when a film is dubbed and the picture stays, the text on screen needs translating. So a forced German track without German audio is almost always a mistake: most likely it was made for a German-dubbed version that isn’t in this file. Unknown audio (und) is flagged too: tag the audio’s language first.

An audio track tagged und (language unknown), or with no language tag at all. Players and Plex pick the audio and subtitle tracks by language — the one matching your settings, or the forced subtitles that go with the audio — so an unknown one gets picked wrongly or not at all. A track with no tag is worse than it looks: Matroska’s rule, which ffmpeg (and so Plex), VLC and mpv all follow, is that an untagged track is English, so every player takes it for English and picks it as such; right only if it is, and then it should say so. A lossy track encoded below what its codec needs for the quality level chosen beside this, per channel (stereo: twice). Each codec has its own floor — MP3 needs the most, Opus the least — and the level scales them all alike: “Only clearly poor” (as it ships) flags MP3 under 128 kbps stereo, AAC or Vorbis under 85, Opus under 64; “Fair” MP3 192, AAC 128, Opus 96; “Good” and “Transparent” raise the bar further. Lossless codecs — FLAC, ALAC, PCM — are never flagged. The bitrate is the file’s, as Plex reads it; the codec from the file itself or its extension.

A video’s audio track in a format most Plex clients can’t play as it is — Dolby TrueHD, DTS-HD Master Audio, DTS, Apple Lossless, PCM — where a FLAC version would play everywhere at about the same size or less. What Plex does with such a track: unless the client (or a receiver behind it, with passthrough on) decodes the format, Plex transcodes the audio to AAC or AC-3, lossy, at a bitrate cut to fit the stream’s quality setting — so a lossless track that can’t be played is heard lossy, and your bandwidth and the server’s CPU go on the transcode. FLAC is decoded by every current Plex client, so a FLAC track direct plays. Named here: TrueHD (FLAC comes out about the same size), DTS-HD MA (a tenth smaller), Apple Lossless (the same), PCM (half), and DTS (a stereo track shrinks; a 5.1 track at 1.5 Mbps grows to about twice — said per track from the bitrate Plex read). Dolby Atmos and DTS:X tracks are left alone: their object metadata doesn’t survive, and they’re what a receiver setup is for. What’s lost otherwise: a legacy receiver that decodes DTS or TrueHD itself gets PCM from the player instead, which some setups can’t pass through.

Audio that FLAC would hold — the very same sound, bit for bit — in less space. PCM (WAV, AIFF, a raw PCM track, a Blu-ray rip’s LPCM): not compressed at all; FLAC (.flac, and inside an MKV), Apple Lossless or WavPack hold it in about half the space, and every player and Plex read them. DTS-HD Master Audio, in a video: FLAC comes out a tenth or so smaller, and every Plex client plays it directly, where DTS-HD is transcoded by many — a phone, a browser, a TV app — and at a lower bitrate the same stream fits a limited upload for remote viewers, which can be the difference between a transcode and a direct stream. DTS (the lossy core, and DTS-HD High Resolution) is judged per track, from the bitrate Plex read against what FLAC would need for its channels and bit depth: a 1.5 Mbps stereo track shrinks to about 0.9 Mbps and is flagged; a 5.1 track at the same bitrate would grow to about twice and isn’t. What FLAC wouldn’t shrink isn’t flagged: Dolby TrueHD comes out about the same size; the other lossy tracks — AC-3, E-AC-3, AAC, MP3 — would get bigger, since FLAC keeps every bit of what the lossy decoder gives, which is more than the track held. Dolby Atmos and DTS:X tracks are left alone too: their object metadata doesn’t survive re-encoding, and the app takes a 7.1 DTS-HD or TrueHD track, or one named for them, to carry it. What’s lost in re-encoding: a legacy receiver that decodes DTS itself gets PCM from the player instead, which some setups can’t pass through; modern hardware doesn’t mind.

Audio that FLAC would hold — the very same sound, bit for bit — in less space. PCM (WAV, AIFF, a raw PCM track, a Blu-ray rip’s LPCM): not compressed at all; FLAC (.flac, and inside an MKV), Apple Lossless or WavPack hold it in about half the space, and every player and Plex read them. DTS-HD Master Audio, in a video: FLAC comes out a tenth or so smaller, and every Plex client plays it directly, where DTS-HD is transcoded by many — a phone, a browser, a TV app — and at a lower bitrate the same stream fits a limited upload for remote viewers, which can be the difference between a transcode and a direct stream.
